couros.name: Couros Zone
couros.short: A tanning quarter on the Couros stream: hides were worked here from the 13th century, and its granite vats still stand
couros.long: The Couros quarter runs along the stream of the same name, west of Guimarães' historic centre. Leather was being worked here by the 13th century: the tanners needed water, and the smell pushed the trade outside the town walls. In the 19th century Couros became the leading leather-processing centre in northern Portugal, and its granite tanning vats, drying sheds and brick factory chimneys survive. In 1977 it became the first industrial-archaeology monument listed in Portugal, and in 2023 it was added to the UNESCO site. Today the old workshops house the Design Institute, a science centre and a youth hostel.
couros.history:
Leather working in Guimarães is documented from the 13th century. The trade needed plenty of water, so the tanners settled not inside the walls but in the low ground along the stream, where water was abundant and the smells did not trouble the townspeople. The stream, once called Ribeira da Costa, gradually took the name Couros — from the Portuguese word for hides. Tanners and curriers worked in pits, vats, presses and on scraping boards; oak bark, once it had given up its tannin, was burned as fuel and spread as fertiliser on the fields.

In the 19th century the area we now call Couros became a privileged centre of hide processing, its output still based on traditional technique and hand labour. Factories went up with their typical drying sheds and granite vats for tanning and dyeing. The first attempts at mechanisation came only in the early 20th century, yet the trade stayed alive until the middle of the century and made Guimarães a national reference in the leather sector.

In July 1977 the Couros Zone was listed as an Imóvel de Interesse Público. It was the first piece of legislation of its kind in Portugal devoted to industrial archaeology: it recognised the value of the leather trade and helped preserve its physical traces.

By the end of the 20th century the industry had faded and the quarter had grown poor. In 2001 Couros was included in the buffer zone of the UNESCO World Heritage site. That same year a multifunctional complex opened, housing a youth hostel, a cybercentre and the Fraterna social cooperative. In 2006 the municipality and the University of Minho launched CampUrbis, a programme to regenerate ten hectares of the quarter. The restored factories found new life as a youth hostel, the Design Institute, an advanced-studies centre and a science centre.

In 2021 the process began to extend the World Heritage boundary over the Couros Zone, and on 19 September 2023 UNESCO approved the extension and the new name: the Historic Centre of Guimarães and Couros Zone. The granite vats and the stream are still the heart of the quarter.

couros.tip: Couros is an open urban area, free to walk. Head west from the centre along Rua de Couros, following the stream: the tanning vats and old factories lie on both sides of the street. On the way, look in on the neighbouring São Francisco monastery and the science centre. The Martins Sarmento Society sometimes runs a themed route from São Crispim to the old tanneries. It pairs well with a walk to the city park; parts of the quarter are still fenced off for regeneration.
